1. Design a real-time peer-to-peer payment system like Zelle, where money moves between banks in seconds, 24/7. How do you guarantee a payment is never debited without being credited when the receiving bank's response times out?

2. Design card fraud detection for tens of millions of debit and credit transactions a day. How do you score every swipe in under 100ms without declining customers who just landed in another country?

4. Design the pipeline that produces daily regulatory and stress-test reports from hundreds of upstream systems. How do you prove the numbers are complete, and reproduce exactly what was submitted a year ago?

5. Design a mobile banking login and session system used by tens of millions of customers. How do you handle device trust, step-up authentication, and instant session revocation when an account is compromised?

6. Design the migration of core deposit accounts from a mainframe to microservices with zero downtime. How do you keep balances consistent while both systems are live?

2. A Kafka consumer processing payment events commits offsets before processing finishes, and a crash silently drops payments. How do you fix the commit strategy without reprocessing everything on restart?

3. An end-of-day batch job that used to finish in 3 hours now takes 8 and is threatening the market-open cutoff. Walk through how you'd diagnose it.

4. An endpoint has p99 latency of 3 seconds while p50 is 60ms, and thread dumps show threads blocked on one synchronized block. How do you find and remove the contention?

5. Your service calls three downstream systems in sequence, and one intermittently hangs for 30 seconds and drags every request down with it. How do you design timeouts, retries, and a circuit breaker so one slow dependency can't take you down?

🏦 5 Major Banks Just Quietly Shifted AI Agent Hack Liability Onto YOU — Read the Fine Print

Your bank just rewrote the rules — and most people have no idea.

This week, Citi, PNC, and Citizens Bank updated their terms of service to make one thing crystal clear:

If you use a third-party AI agent to manage your finances and something goes wrong — you're on your own. 🚨

And we're not just talking about the AI making a bad transaction.

We're talking about:
→ The AI agent leaking your banking credentials
→ A hacker breaking INTO the AI tool and draining your account
→ Any unauthorized transaction made by an automated assistant

All of it? YOUR liability. Not the bank's.

Here's the full picture of where things stand right now:

🔴 JPMorgan — adopted this policy last month
🔴 Bank of America — adopted this policy last month
🔴 Citi — updated terms this week
🔴 PNC — updated terms this week
🔴 Citizens Bank — emailed customers this week

That's 5 of the biggest banks in the US, all moving in the same direction — fast.

Citi does carve out one narrow exception: AI agents that THEY provide directly won't trigger the extra liability. Convenient, right?

Here's what this really signals 👇

Banks aren't just worried about security. They're worried about losing control of the customer relationship.

AI-powered personal finance tools can help users avoid unnecessary fees, find better interest rates, and automate bill payments. That's a direct threat to bank margins.

So the message is clear: use OUR AI, or bear the risk yourself.

Even Anthropic's Claude launched its personal finance tool this month as "read-only" — it can't move or invest your money. That's not a coincidence.

This is part of a broader pattern we're seeing across industries. AI labs promise agents will revolutionize how we interact with services. Then the service providers say "hold on."

We've seen it with Uber. We've seen it with DoorDash. Now we're seeing it with banking.

The consumer protection implications here are massive — and regulators haven't caught up yet.

⚠️ Bottom line: Before you connect any AI tool to your bank account, read the fine print. The liability landscape just changed dramatically.

What do you think — should banks be allowed to push hack liability onto customers for third-party AI tools? Or is this a consumer protection crisis waiting to happen?

Bank of America had to email its customers: stop giving your banking passwords to your AI agents. And when you do, you're on your own!

They’re right, though. It’s not an AI problem. It’s an onboarding problem.

You wouldn’t hand a new employee your master key on day one.

You’d say: “Here’s what you can touch and here’s what you can’t. Check with me before doing anything crazy.”

That’s not distrust. That’s how good teams function.

AI agents are the newest members of the team. Same rules apply:

- Access scoped to the task, not the whole house
- A log of everything they did
- A human who signs off on the big decisions.

Guardrails aren’t the brakes. They exist so you can drive fast knowing when to slow down, or stop.

Five Days. Five Outages. Zero Shots Fired.

In World War II, it took bombers to bring a country to a standstill.
In 2026, it just takes a bad update.
No shots were fired this week, yet look at what went dark across the U.S.:
• Thursday: Outlook and Teams went down across 74 countries for nearly 24 hours.
• Friday: 10,000+ flights were grounded for 4 hours.
• Monday: Major banks—JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, Bank of America, and Zelle—were hit by outages.
• Tuesday morning: Even the NSA’s classified network was paralyzed.
• Tuesday before lunch: iCloud, Apple Pay, and the App Store crashed simultaneously, logging users out worldwide.
The official causes? A "software defect." A router upgrade. A routine patch. Apple hasn't even given a reason yet.
This highlights a terrifying vulnerability in modern infrastructure: single points of failure.
A traditional war has to break through an army. Today, whether it’s a cyberattack or simple human error, disruption only needs to break through one centralized system—one cloud, one banking rail, one air traffic network.
If the most trusted names in tech and defense can go dark on an ordinary Tuesday, our reliance on centralized systems has become our biggest national security risk.
Coincidence, systemic fragility, or silent warfare—what do you think is really driving this wave of outages?

Your bank just decided who pays when your AI agent gets it wrong. It isn't the bank.

This week Citibank rewrote its Online User Agreement so anything a third-party AI agent does with your account counts as your act - including losses after the agent leaks your credentials or gets hacked. PNC changed its terms on 18 November. Citizens emailed customers the same warning. JPMorgan and Bank of America moved in October, and Wells Fargo's version takes effect 24 November.

Read that as a product decision, not a legal one.

Under Regulation E, an unauthorized transfer is capped at $50 if you report it within two business days. But a transaction your agent "authorized" is not unauthorized. The banks are not arguing about fraud - they are reclassifying the agent's action as yours, which moves the loss outside the cap before any dispute starts.

Now put that next to the adoption numbers. Uber handled roughly 320 million trips and orders in Halloween week; third-party agents placed about 500 Uber Eats orders and four rides in Q3. DoorDash has taken "several hundred" agent orders in total. The agentic web is not blocked by model quality. It is blocked by who holds the loss.

That is the pattern of 2026: labs ship capability, incumbents ship terms. Uber, DoorDash, the banks - each answers the same question in its own contract, and the answer is "not us."

The operator read: if you build agents that touch money, identity or inventory, your hardest engineering problem is now a liability architecture problem. Read-only is a feature. Scoped credentials are a feature. An audit trail your counterparty accepts is the moat.

The agents that win will not be the smartest. They will be the ones someone is willing to be responsible for.

#AI #TechNews #Innovation #Business #Finance

#America250 Spotlight! 🇺🇸🇮🇹
 
As we continue commemorating America’s 250th anniversary, we celebrate Amadeo Pietro Giannini, an Italian American visionary whose innovation helped reshape the nation’s banking system and expand opportunity for millions.
 
Born in San Jose, California, to Italian immigrant parents, Giannini founded the Bank of Italy in San Francisco in 1904 with a mission to serve everyday Americans, including immigrants, working families, and small business owners who were often overlooked by traditional financial institutions.
 
After the devastating 1906 San Francisco earthquake, Giannini helped the city rebuild by providing loans to residents when many banks were unable to operate. His belief that access to capital could help communities thrive transformed the banking industry and eventually led to the creation of Bank of America.
 
Giannini’s legacy reflects the entrepreneurial spirit and contributions of Italian Americans throughout our nation’s history. As we celebrate America’s 250th anniversary, we honor the innovators and community leaders whose vision helped build the United States we know today. 🇺🇸🇮🇹

The shift?

Canada finally joining the instant-payments club is less about being late and more about who's rushing to use it. The Real-Time Rail arrives years after Brazil's Pix, India's UPI and the US's FedNow, a reminder that even a rich, advanced economy can lag when its banking market is comfortable and concentrated. And that's the real story here. Notice who's first in line: Wealthsimple and KOHO, the challengers, while Canada's big banks are joining "in stages." That split tells you everything. Instant rails are an equalizer, they let a FinTech move money as fast as any incumbent, without needing branches or a card empire, which is exactly why the challengers are eager and the giants are in no hurry. In one of the developed world's most protected banking markets, real-time payments could be the thing that finally lets challengers compete on level ground. The infrastructure is boring. What it unlocks, in a market this concentrated, is not.

Does Canada's long-delayed real-time rail finally give challengers like Wealthsimple a real shot at the big banks, or will the incumbents' dominance hold even on a level playing field?

Citi already decided what happens next. It rewrote its terms this week: everything your agent does counts as you doing it. Wrong transfer? Yours. Agent gets hacked and the account gets drained? Still yours.

JPMorgan and Bank of America did the same last month. PNC and Citizens joined this week. Wells Fargo's version lands Nov 24. Five banks, one message.

The part nobody mentions: the bank's own AI tools don't carry this liability. Only the agent you chose does.

And the law is silent. Regulation E caps what you owe on unauthorised transfers, but no court has ruled whether a hijacked agent counts as unauthorised.

So the fight is simple. Your agent, your loss. Or banks can't sign away fraud protection in the fine print.

🔹 Connect customer due diligence with actual transaction behavior.
🔹 Treat sanctions screening as a continuously evolving control.

The real measure of a compliance program is not the controls it claims to have, but the risks it can demonstrably detect and prevent.

Over the past month, Citi, JPMorgan, Bank of America, Morgan Stanley and Schwab have restricted outside AI agents from acting on customer accounts. Citi still allows read-only access through approved open-banking providers.

That last detail is the interesting part. The banks haven't drawn the line at AI. They've drawn it at write access.

My read: this is an authorisation problem more than an AI problem. Many agents today get into a bank account the crude way, with the customer's own username and password. To the bank, the agent is the customer. It carries every permission the person has, it can't be revoked on its own, and nobody can tell afterwards whether a transfer came from the human or the software. Reports of agents going beyond what customers asked are what you'd expect from that setup.

When designing tool-calling workflows, one architectural decision I've found important is treating every tool as a permission boundary, not just a function the model can call. 
Applied to agents and bank accounts, that would look something like:

1. Delegated credentials, not shared ones. The agent gets its own scoped, short-lived, revocable token, so the user can cut it off without changing their password.

2. Policy enforced outside the model. Limits like "move at most ₹10,000, only between my own accounts" live in a server-side policy layer. A prompt is not a security boundary.

3. Reads and writes treated differently. Reading balances can be fairly open. Anything that moves money needs explicit confirmation from the human.

4. Traceable actions. Every request carries the agent's identity and the user's original instruction, so disputes and liability have an audit trail.

5. Idempotency and a kill switch. A retry shouldn't send a payment twice, and the bank should be able to shut down one misbehaving agent without blocking everyone.

None of this is new. Most of it already exists for third-party apps. What's missing is a standard agents can plug into, which is why blocking is the sensible default for now.

My guess is that the first bank to offer proper agent credentials will gain deposits from this shift, not lose them.

So who should set that standard: the banks, regulators, or the agent platforms?
